mcqs.question: A card paints itself with `background: var(--surface)` and `color: var(--surface-contrast)`. Theme switching sets `data-theme="dark"` on `<html>` at runtime, and one card overrides the pair with `style="--surface: #f5f5f5"`. All three behaviours work with no rebuild: the page repaints, the themed subtree gets the dark pair, and that one card keeps its own surface. Which mechanism explains them?
options: `var(--surface)` is substituted at build time, so switching themes ships several compiled stylesheets and the attribute picks which one loads.
Custom properties are declarations that inherit, and `var()` is substituted per element at computed-value time; `:root` is only the top of that chain, so a nearer declaration wins.
Unregistered custom properties are untyped, so the engine cannot resolve them; `@property` registration is what makes `var(--surface)` produce a value instead of falling back.
`--surface` on `:root` is a document-wide constant: descendants inherit the resolved value, so nothing below the root can override it after the first paint.
mcqs.explanation: The declaration `--surface: #fff` is a declaration like any other: it participates in the cascade, it inherits, and `var(--surface)` is substituted on each element at computed-value time with the value that element ended up with. That single mechanism explains all three observations. The `[data-theme="dark"]` block redeclares the pair on `<html>`, every descendant inherits those declarations and re-resolves `background`/`color`, so the repaint needs no stylesheet work. The inline `--surface` on one card is a declaration on the element itself, nearer than the inherited value, so that card keeps `#f5f5f5` while still inheriting `--surface-contrast`. Nothing was frozen at build time, which is why an attribute flip is enough (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Cascading_variables/Using_custom_properties, https://www.w3.org/TR/css-variables-1/). The strongest distractor is the build-time substitution: `--x` looks like Sass, so engineers assume the value was baked into the rule, and that belief is what produces per-theme compiled stylesheets and `!important` theme patches. Option 2 turns 'untyped' into 'unresolvable': unregistered custom properties are valid and substitute normally, and `@property` only adds syntax, inheritance control and an initial value. Option 3 freezes inheritance at the root, which would make any subtree override require a new component variant.

mcqs.question: A normal author rule in `@layer app` conflicts with a normal unlayered author rule. Which normally has higher precedence?
options: The layered rule, because layers always override unlayered CSS.
The rule with the more specific selector, regardless of layer.
The unlayered rule, before specificity is compared.
The rule that appears first in the source.
mcqs.explanation: For normal author declarations, unlayered styles outrank layered styles, so the cascade can discard the layered candidate before specificity. The best distractor is option 1: specificity matters only after origin and layer precedence are tied.

mcqs.question: What is the role of `color-scheme: light dark`?
options: It automatically rewrites every authored color in the document.
It declares that the element can be rendered in both schemes and lets user-agent UI adapt.
It permanently selects dark mode even when the user prefers light.
It replaces `prefers-color-scheme` for authored component styles.
mcqs.explanation: `color-scheme` advertises supported schemes and lets browser UI such as controls and scrollbars adapt. Authored content still needs its own theme rules, commonly using `prefers-color-scheme` or a selector. Option 0 is the most plausible misconception: the property does not rewrite arbitrary authored colors.

mcqs.question: A theme client keeps a `light` / `dark` / `system` preference in `localStorage`. On load it applies `stored ?? (mql.matches ? 'dark' : 'light')`, then registers `mql.addEventListener('change', () => { const next = mql.matches ? 'dark' : 'light'; apply(next); localStorage.setItem('theme', next); })` with `mql = matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')`. A user picks `light` at noon; that evening the OS flips to dark, the page turns dark, and the picker now shows `dark`. What is the defect?
options: The `MediaQueryList` is a snapshot taken at load, so the handler must call `matchMedia` again; re-querying inside the callback would also stop the write-back.
The handler ignores the preference and overwrites it with the resolved value; it must act only while the preference is `system`, and never persist the result.
`localStorage` writes are asynchronous, so the listener's write lands after the picker reads the key and the UI shows the value it wrote over.
`change` fires only for an explicit `light` or `dark` preference, so the defect is the picker reading `data-theme` instead of the stored key.
mcqs.explanation: Two defects compound, and both come from collapsing two values into one. `system` is a preference, not a theme: while it is selected the resolved theme must follow `prefers-color-scheme`, and an explicit `light`/`dark` must outrank the OS. The listener does neither — it fires on every OS change, applies the resolved value even though the user chose `light`, and then persists that resolved value, so the next load reads `dark` as if the user had asked for it (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/matchMedia, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/At-rules/%40media/prefers-color-scheme). The fix keeps the stored preference untouched, resolves on read, and guards the handler with `if (readPreference() === 'system')`. The strongest distractor is the snapshot claim: a `MediaQueryList` is live, `mql.matches` is current inside the handler, and re-querying changes nothing — it reads as plausible because `matchMedia()` looks like a one-off call. Option 2 confuses async semantics: `localStorage.setItem` has completed by the time the next statement reads the key. Option 3 inverts when `change` fires.

mcqs.question: Which is the strongest public styling contract for a reusable Button?
options: Consumers must target the generated `.css-8f2a` class.
Consumers may depend on the component's current nested `<span>` structure.
Consumers use documented variants, sizes, states, and deliberate slots.
Consumers copy the component stylesheet and edit it locally.
mcqs.explanation: Semantic variants, states, and slots describe intentional API surface and can survive internal markup or engine changes. Options 0 and 1 couple consumers to implementation details; option 3 forks the system instead of creating a supported extension point.

mcqs.question: A two-brand token set defines `blue.600`, `color.text.primary` aliased to `{color.blue.600}`, and `button.primary.background` aliased to `{color.text.primary}`. Brand B re-points `color.text.primary` at `teal.700`: the button renders teal, but a new `Badge` whose token was authored as `{color.blue.600}` still renders blue. What does that expose?
options: The Badge needs a brand-specific primitive so brand B has something to override; aliasing a primitive is what keeps component values traceable.
The Badge skipped the semantic level: a component token should alias a role, so one brand map re-points every consumer instead of each component needing a branch.
Themes are expected to override component tokens, so the fix is a `[data-brand="b"]` block that redeclares `badge.background` next to the button entry.
The semantic level is redundant once component tokens exist; collapsing the two levels makes the brand override reach the palette directly.
mcqs.explanation: The hierarchy is primitive -> semantic -> component, and the direction of each alias is what makes a theme a value map instead of a fork. Components consume roles; a brand or a color mode re-points the roles and every consumer follows. The Badge skipped that level: its token points at a raw scale entry, so no theme can reach it without naming the Badge (https://www.designtokens.org/TR/2025.10/format/, https://www.w3.org/community/design-tokens). The fix is to alias a semantic role (`color.text.primary`, or a more specific `badge.text` if the badge genuinely diverges), then let both brand maps decide its value. The strongest distractor is the traceability argument: pointing at a primitive feels more honest, but it parks the decision below the level themes operate on, and 'one primitive per brand per component' reproduces the per-brand branch at the bottom of the tree. Option 2 works for this one badge and needs a new entry in every brand block for every component — exactly the fork the hierarchy prevents. Option 3 deletes the level that carries the theming contract.

mcqs.question: Release 3.1.0 renames `--color-action-accent` to `--color-action-primary` and ships as a patch, arguing that no prop, export or TypeScript type changed. Consumers on 3.x then report primary buttons with a transparent background: their CSS still reads `var(--color-action-accent)` with no fallback. What is the correct classification, and what signal was missed?
options: Patch is correct: custom properties are styling details, and SemVer covers the documented component API, not the CSS a component happens to emit.
Major: a published custom-property name is part of the contract, and a missing custom property invalidates the declaration instead of throwing, so no type check sees it.
Minor: a rename is a deprecation, so it belongs in a minor with a changelog entry and the old name removed only in the next major release.
Patch is acceptable as long as a codemod ships with it, because a mechanical migration makes the rename non-breaking for consumers.
mcqs.explanation: SemVer classifies by what happens to a consumer who upgrades, not by which files the change touched. A documented `--color-*` name is authored by consumers, so renaming it breaks their CSS; `var()` against a missing custom property makes the declaration invalid at computed-value time, so `background` falls back to its initial value — transparent — with no error and nothing for TypeScript to see. That silent failure is exactly the class of break the deprecation rule exists for: ship `--color-action-primary` and keep the old name as an alias in a minor, mark it deprecated, remove it in a major (https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html, https://www.designtokens.org/TR/2025.10/format/#deprecated). The strongest distractor is option 0, because it is the reasoning that produced the patch: 'tokens are internals' holds only for tokens nobody documented or consumed. Option 2 confuses a deprecation schedule with a version class — the alias is the minor, the removal is the major. Option 3 lowers the cost of migrating but does not fix consumers who never ran the codemod.

mcqs.question: A shared package publishes `dist.css`, compiled by Tailwind from app A's sources. App B imports it, and its own `lg:p-6` and `text-brand` render unstyled; any token change also needs a package rebuild and release. What is the correct structure?
options: Register every consumer's source paths with `@source` in the package stylesheet so the shared build emits the union of the utilities those apps use.
Publish the theme as `@theme` CSS with tokens only and let each app import it after `tailwindcss` and compile its own utilities, with Tailwind as a peer.
Compile once with no source scan and ship every utility Tailwind can generate, so any app can use any class from the shared file.
Move `tailwindcss` into the package dependencies and re-export its config, so all apps share one compiler and one generated stylesheet.
mcqs.explanation: Utilities encode one app's source scan and one compiler version, so they are the wrong artifact to share; tokens are the vocabulary that survives both. Tailwind's own guidance is a `@theme` file each project imports, placed after `tailwindcss`, so every build generates exactly the classes its own sources use (https://tailwindcss.com/docs/theme#sharing-across-projects, https://tailwindcss.com/docs/detecting-classes-in-source-files). Import order is part of the contract: the shared theme comes before the app's own `@theme` block, so a local deviation overrides a value instead of being overridden. The strongest distractor is `@source`: it is a real directive and it would make app B's classes appear, but only by making the package build depend on every consumer's tree — it cannot know future consumers, it still pins one compiler version for everyone, and it inverts ownership. Option 2 ships every utility: bundle cost, and the file still goes stale when an app upgrades Tailwind. Option 3 shares the compiler rather than the decisions, which is the version coupling the split exists to avoid.

mcqs.question: A runtime CSS-in-JS engine passes local review but misbehaves in production SSR: a base style wins for one frame before the override lands, a `style-src 'nonce-...'` policy blocks injected tags on some routes, and server and client HTML list the style tags in a different order. Which evaluation question would have surfaced all three?
options: Whether the engine generates unique, stable class names, since name collisions are what make overrides order-dependent.
Whether it extracts and orders styles deterministically on the server, emits them under the CSP nonce, and adds no work beyond hydration.
Whether the engine supports prop-driven styles, since only a runtime engine can turn arbitrary prop values into CSS.
Whether the output is atomic, since atomic classes are what keep the server and the client style order identical.
mcqs.explanation: All three symptoms are properties of the emitted output, and none is about how the styles look. Precedence among injected rules follows document order, so an engine that injects during render can emit a different order on the server than on the client: the override arrives after the base rule, and the frame before it paints the base. CSP sees each injected `<style>` element and inline `style` attribute, so an engine without an extraction-plus-nonce story fails at runtime, not at build. And creating styles per mount is work the first paint did not need. That is why the question has to cover extraction, deterministic order, nonces and runtime cost together (https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/style). The strongest distractor is unique class names: uniqueness stops two components from colliding, but it says nothing about which of their rules lands first, and hashed names are unstable across builds — an API problem, not this one. Atomic output is a real optimization and often deterministic, yet atomicity is not the guarantee; extraction plus a fixed order is. Prop-driven styles are the actual reason to accept a runtime, so that question describes the cost, not the mitigation.

mcqs.question: A design-system dashboard reports 84 components, 1,240 stories at 92% snapshot coverage, and a 310 kB CSS bundle. A product lead asks which number predicts whether the next major release will be safe and worth the migration. Which set actually answers that?
options: Component count against the design tool's library, because parity is what makes the system complete enough to adopt.
Share of product UI on system components, upgrade success per release, and accessibility regressions found after the bump.
Story count and snapshot percentage, because coverage of rendered states is the closest available regression signal.
Generated CSS size, because a smaller bundle proves teams dropped local styles and adopted the shared tokens.
mcqs.explanation: The signals that predict a release are outcomes in consuming teams: how much product UI actually uses the system, whether upgrades land without incident, and whether accessibility regresses afterwards. Those are the metrics the operating model names, and they move when the system is useful rather than merely large (https://www.greatfrontend.com/front-end-system-design-playbook/types-of-questions, https://design-system.w3.org/). The strongest distractor is story and snapshot coverage: it reads like test coverage, but it measures inventory plus self-comparison — 1,240 snapshots diffed against their own previous output pass while the component ships a broken keyboard flow no story drives, and a story set of happy paths inflates the percentage. Component count (0) is the vanity metric: inventory grows without adoption. CSS size (3) moves for unrelated reasons, and a bundle can shrink by deleting components nobody used.

mcqs.question: A `Menu` has two stories: `Open`, with `args: { open: true }`, and `KeyboardClose`, which opens the menu and asserts `aria-expanded="false"` after pressing Escape, inside a `play` function. A regression makes Escape a no-op. CI runs the Storybook test runner with the a11y addon and a visual runner. What fails, and why?
options: Both stories, because the a11y addon re-scans the DOM after every interaction and flags the dead key handler.
`KeyboardClose` only: the `play` function drives the interaction and asserts the result, while `Open` renders a static state and never presses Escape.
Neither, unless stories are also excluded from the production bundle, which is what the test runner requires.
`Open`, because its Controls panel re-runs the args on every change and asserts the resulting rendered output.
mcqs.explanation: A `play` function runs in the browser after the story renders: it can press keys, click, and assert the resulting DOM, so `KeyboardClose` is the only artifact that executes the Escape path and fails when the handler dies (https://storybook.js.org/docs/writing-tests/interaction-testing, https://storybook.js.org/docs/writing-stories/play-function). The other two mechanisms cannot see it: the visual runner diffs pixels of the state each story renders, and `Open` only ever renders the open state; the a11y addon checks rule violations in the rendered DOM, and no rule knows your menu is supposed to close on Escape. The strongest distractor is the Controls claim: Controls are a manual args editor in the docs UI, they do not run in CI and they assert nothing. Option 0 invents an automatic re-scan per event, and option 2 confuses a normal build optimization (stories excluded from the app bundle) with a test-runner requirement.

mcqs.question: A card title is sized with `font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2vw, 2.5rem)`. Reviewers report the title renders at the same size in a 20rem sidebar and in a 60rem content grid, and they want it to grow with the space the card actually gets. What causes that, and what is the minimal correct change?
options: Nothing is wrong with the approach: `clamp()` measures the parent's width, so the two placements differ only once the min or max bound is crossed.
The mixed-unit sum `1rem + 2vw` is not a valid `<calc-sum>`, so the declaration is dropped and the title inherits the root size in both placements; write the middle term as a single unit.

`2vw` resolves against the viewport, so where the card is placed never enters the calculation; establish a query container with `container-type: inline-size` and put a container unit such as `cqi` in the preferred term.
`clamp()` applies the minimum before the preferred term is evaluated, so the title stays pinned at `1.5rem` until the viewport passes the max; the fix is to drop the bounds.
mcqs.explanation: `vw` is a viewport unit: the preferred term `1rem + 2vw` produces one computed value for a given viewport, so a 20rem sidebar and a 60rem grid column render the identical size — placement is invisible to the formula. To make the value follow the space the component receives, an ancestor must be a query container (`container-type: inline-size`, or the shorthand `container: card / inline-size`), and the preferred term must use a container query length unit such as `cqi` (1% of the container's inline size). One caveat worth stating in review: an element's own `container-type` does not serve its own units — an element is not its own query container, so the units on the card resolve against an ancestor container and fall back to the small viewport size when there is none (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_containment/Container_queries, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Values/clamp). The strongest distractor is the mixed-unit claim: `clamp()`/`calc()` accept any `<calc-sum>`, and adding `rem` to `vw` is valid — the result is a length computed from both. It is a tempting answer because the declaration does look precarious, but it is the viewport reference, not unit mixing, that makes placement irrelevant. The bound-ordering distractor fails too: `clamp()` compares the preferred value against the bounds after computing it, and the title is not pinned at the minimum here — it sits at whatever the viewport-derived value gives, often at the maximum in a wide window.

mcqs.question: A design system ships this as its complete reduced-motion policy: `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { *, *::before, *::after { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; } }`. Which critique of that policy is the accurate one?
options: It is already the recommended policy; adding `scroll-behavior: auto` to the same block would complete it, and per-component reduced rules would only duplicate the timings.

It is a timing override rather than a policy: infinite animations keep looping as near-instant cycles, movement that carried meaning (a drawer sliding in, a shake marking an error) is neither removed nor replaced by a non-motion equivalent, and because it bypasses the duration and easing tokens no component can express "instant, or opacity-only, same information, focus and status still visible".

It fails because `transition-duration` cannot be overridden with `!important` once a component declared the `transition` shorthand, so the second declaration is ignored and transitions still run at full speed.
It fails only under `forced-colors: active`, where timing overrides are dropped along with shadows and background images.
mcqs.explanation: The block is an engine-wide timing patch with no semantic content. It does not distinguish essential from decorative movement, so an infinite `animation` keeps iterating — only extremely fast, which for a vestibular-sensitive user is not "no motion". It also strips the informational job motion was doing (the drawer's direction, the error shake) without substituting the non-motion equivalent the bank's policy requires: an instant state change, an opacity transition, a persisting error icon and message. And by reaching around the motion tokens, it makes the per-component decision — which the system is supposed to own — inexpressible (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/At-rules/@media/prefers-reduced-motion, https://www.w3.org/TR/mediaqueries-5/). Model motion as semantic duration and easing tokens, then let each component declare its reduced form with the reduced rule as the final override. The strongest distractor is option 0: the near-zero-duration blanket is repeated in a lot of accessibility advice and it does neutralize the worst offenders, so it reads as settled. It is a useful triage layer, not a policy — it answers "how long" for every animation and never answers "which movement is optional, and what replaces it". The shorthand-transition distractor is factually wrong: `transition-duration` is a longhand, and an `!important` longhand beats a non-important shorthand declaration. The forced-colors distractor confuses two unrelated media features; forced colors changes colors, not timing.

mcqs.question: A design system exposes `--focus-ring` and every control ships `.control:focus-visible { outline: none; box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px var(--focus-ring); }`. Keyboard users on Windows high contrast / forced-colors mode report they can no longer see where focus is. What is the root cause and the system-level fix?
options: Custom properties stop being inherited in forced-colors mode, so `--focus-ring` resolves to nothing; redeclare the token inside the `forced-colors` media query.
`:focus-visible` is not honored in forced-colors mode, so every control has to be switched to `:focus` and the token kept as a shadow.
Forced colors only repaints colors and never removes shadows, so the ring is still painted but is hidden behind the `outline: none` reset; the fix is to give `box-shadow` a higher z-index token.

Forced colors drops author `box-shadow`, and because `outline: none` was authored there is nothing left — the UA does not restore the ring. The fix is for the focus token to be an `outline` (system colors such as `Highlight`/`CanvasText` survive forced colors), with a `forced-colors: active` block reserved for local adjustments.
mcqs.explanation: In forced-colors mode the engine forces a limited system palette and discards author effects it cannot re-map — `box-shadow` and background images among them — while keeping `outline`, which it recolors. This system removed the outline and moved the entire indicator into the discarded effect, so the author has painted nothing and the UA has no default to fall back on: the author declaration is what wins, and forced colors does not roll it back (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/At-rules/@media/forced-colors, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Selectors/:focus-visible). The durable fix is structural: the focus token is an outline width/style plus a system color (`Highlight`), so the indicator survives recoloring and forced colors by construction, and per-component `forced-colors` blocks only fix genuinely lost affordances such as a shadow that signalled elevation. The strongest distractor is option 2 — "forced colors only repaints colors" is the belief that keeps teams shipping `box-shadow` focus rings, and its fix (z-index on a shadow) is not a thing. Option 0 confuses inheritance with forcing: custom properties inherit exactly as in any other mode; what breaks is the shadow they feed. Option 1 inverts the selector story — `:focus-visible` works fine there, and `box-shadow` is precisely the wrong channel.

mcqs.question: Mid-migration you wrap the design system's CSS in `@layer system` and leave the legacy stylesheet unlayered, loaded by a `<link>` in the app shell. Migrated markup is `<div class="card ds-card">`, the legacy file still contains `.panel .card { padding: 8px }`, and the DS rule `.ds-card { padding: 24px }` loses — even where the DS selector is more specific. What is happening, and what is the fix?
options: Unlayered normal author declarations outrank every layer, so the DS cannot win while the legacy CSS stays unlayered; route it into a lower layer (`@import url("legacy.css") layer(legacy);` with the layer order declared up front) or wrap it with `@layer legacy`.
Cascade layers only reorder `!important` declarations, so normal declarations always compete on specificity alone; the DS rule needs a higher-specificity selector.
The layer order follows the order in which stylesheets are linked, so moving the DS stylesheet after the legacy `<link>` places it later in the cascade and fixes the conflict.
`@layer` cannot contain CSS that arrives through `<link>` or `@import`, which is why the legacy rules escape it; the legacy stylesheet has to be inlined into the bundle before layering works.
mcqs.explanation: For normal declarations the cascade compares origin and importance first, then layers, and only then specificity: unlayered author styles sit after every layer, so `.panel .card` wins over any layered rule no matter how specific. That is the trap in an incremental adoption — wrapping only the new code in a layer makes the old code permanently the strongest author CSS. The fix is to put the legacy CSS inside a layer positioned below the system, declared once and early so the order is fixed (`@layer legacy, system, app;`), then import or wrap the vendor/legacy stylesheet into `legacy` (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/At-rules/@layer). With both sides layered, `system` beats `legacy` deterministically and specificity stops being the argument. The strongest distractor is option 2, the "move the file later" reflex: link order only decides where a rule lands among *unlayered* rules, and reordering cannot give the DS priority over an unlayered legacy rule that keeps winning — that reflex is exactly the habit layers exist to retire. Option 1 reverses the rule (layers do affect normal declarations), and option 3 is false: `@import ... layer(name)` exists precisely to place linked stylesheets into a layer, and `@layer legacy { ... }` wraps imported rules in your own build.

scenarios.prompt: A server-rendered app supports `light`, `dark` and `system`. QA reports four symptoms: (a) users whose OS is dark see a light page for one or two frames on every navigation; (b) React logs a hydration mismatch on the root element; (c) flipping the OS theme with the tab open changes nothing until reload; (d) a user whose stored value was written by an older build as `auto` gets no themed styles at all. Repair the bootstrap and say exactly where the preference/resolved-theme boundary lives.
rubric: Diagnoses the flash as a paint-timing defect and moves the decision into a blocking head script or a server-rendered attribute, not into hydration or an effect.
Separates the persisted `Preference` (including `system`) from the derived `Resolved` theme and never writes the resolved value back as the preference.
Subscribes to the `change` event only while the preference is `system`, and cleans the listener up.
Replaces the `as Preference` cast with validation plus a defined fallback, covering corrupted and blocked storage.
Makes server and client initial attribute agree, declares `color-scheme`, and states a test plan: first paint, OS flip, explicit override, storage failure.

scenarios.prompt: A vendor stylesheet beats your component styles: `.title` inside `.Card` renders red in checkout while Storybook renders it correctly. The vendor rule is `.widget .title { color: red }`; yours is `@layer components { :where(.Card) .title { color: var(--color-text) } }`. Raising your selector to `.Card .title.title` changes nothing. Explain the precedence, then give the layer policy plus the exact CSS and build steps, without adding `!important`.
rubric: States the cascade order (origin and importance, then layer, then specificity) and that unlayered normal declarations sit after every layer.
Fixes it by declaring the layer order once in the entry sheet and routing the vendor CSS into a lower layer, not by raising specificity.
Notes that `@import ... layer()` must precede other rules, or that a `<link>` sheet has to be routed through the build, and checks the built CSS.
Keeps `:where()`/shallow selectors and explains that the layer, not specificity, is doing the work.
Mentions that `!important` reverses layer order and is not the escape hatch.

scenarios.prompt: You are moving a large runtime CSS-in-JS component library to static CSS plus custom properties, and teams must keep shipping. The audit found three couplings: 41 call sites target engine-generated names with descendant selectors (`& .css-1x2y3 { margin-inline-end: 8px }`); the SSR entry injects style tags per render and production HTML carries about 40 kB of duplicated rules; two apps read the theme object from the runtime provider to pick icons. Design the boundary, show the first slice, and state what must be true before the runtime is deleted.
rubric: Preserves the component API and replaces generated class names with documented attributes/tokens instead of trying to reproduce hashes.
Migrates tokens first, then leaves, using adapters with a removal date rather than a flag-day rewrite.
Handles both non-component couplings explicitly: consumer descendant selectors and theme-object reads.
Defines SSR verification (identical server/client markup and style order, no duplicate injection) plus visual and accessibility regression per state and theme.
States measurable completion: runtime chunk gone, bundle delta known, teams shipping throughout.

scenarios.prompt: This card ships fluid type and spacing. Reviewers report three symptoms: (a) the title renders identically in a 20rem sidebar and a 60rem grid column; (b) the card's padding does not respond to the card's width at all; (c) when the card is dropped into a `max-content` chip row, it collapses to zero width. Diagnose each defect, then refactor so the tokens stay the public contract, the component adapts to its own placement, and there is a sane fallback when no container exists.
rubric: Identifies `vw` as the reason the title ignores placement, and replaces the preferred term with a container unit (`cqi`) with `rem` bounds kept for zoom.

Explains that an element's own `container-type` does not serve its own container units — the units resolve against the nearest ancestor container, falling back to the small viewport size when there is none.
Traces the zero-width card to inline-size containment removing content from inline sizing, and moves containment to a slot with a definite inline size instead of the component.
Refactor keeps the fluid formula in semantic tokens, names the container, and does not duplicate raw clamp values inside the component or the query block.
States a verification plan: container-width stories, 200% zoom and long words, narrow viewport, and an explicit static fallback when no container or no container-query support exists.
